kindle_hid_passthrough/ package. Consolidate BLE and Classic hosts into
a unified HIDHost, add Scanner for BLE+Classic discovery, and split
concerns into focused modules (config, daemon, host, scanner,
uhid_handler, device_cache, logging_utils, bt_setup, main).

endpoints for status, scan, pair, connect, disconnect, remove, logs, and
cache management.

hci_transport as a fallback rather than an override.

fix: BLE pairing flow drops connection causing keyboard sleep timeout

After BTManager pairing, the controller destroyed the active BLE
connection and the daemon had to scan from scratch. By then the
keyboard had gone to sleep, requiring a keypress to reconnect.

- Hand off paired HIDHost from controller to daemon instead of
  destroying it, so daemon calls continue_after_pairing() on the
  live connection
- Skip re-encryption on reused pairing connection to avoid SMP
  mismatch that caused CancelledError on first pair attempt
- Check hid_reports (not report_map) to ensure report characteristics
  are discovered for notification subscription
- Add missing _ble_activate_hid_service() to daemon reconnect flow
  so Exit Suspend is written after every reconnection

Closes #34

fix: pair overlay race when scan still holds op_lock

is_pairing was only set after acquiring _op_lock inside the async
coroutine. If a scan was still running, /pair-status polls saw
is_pairing=False and dismissed the overlay before pairing started.

Set is_pairing=True synchronously in request_pair() so status polls
see it immediately regardless of lock contention.

Signed-off-by: Lucas Zampieri <lcasmz54@gmail.com>

fix: BLE reconnection via filter accept list and proper disconnect

BLE reconnection used active scanning which misses directed advertising
from bonded keyboards. Replace with HCI filter accept list approach
where the controller enters the initiating state and catches both
directed and undirected advertising from known devices.

Also fix disconnect button suspending the daemon instead of dropping
the connection — now calls connection.disconnect() directly so the
daemon naturally cycles back to waiting for reconnection.

Signed-off-by: Lucas Zampieri <lcasmz54@gmail.com>

fix: separate stop and disconnect so daemon stop actually stops

Stop and disconnect were both calling suspend(), so when disconnect was
fixed to use connection.disconnect() instead, stop broke. Now they are
separate operations: stop suspends the daemon, disconnect drops the
connection and lets the daemon reconnect.

Also consolidate deploy recipe to always open BTManager.

fix: strip digitizer collections from HID descriptors for UHID

Some BLE devices (e.g. page-turner clickers like the E1 Control) include
Digitizer/multitouch collections alongside Consumer Control in their HID
report descriptors. The Kindle kernel (4.9.77-lab126) has
CONFIG_HID_MULTITOUCH disabled, which causes hid-core to silently refuse
to create any input device for the entire UHID device when it encounters
these collections. Stripping them before UHID_CREATE2 allows hid-generic
to claim the remaining collections normally.

Fixes #45

fix: suppress libenvload.so preload warning in install.sh pair flow

The Kindle's /etc/ld.so.preload references /usr/lib/libenvload.so

daemon and BTManager contexts but left the interactive install.sh

fix: stop reconnect loop and clear pairing keys on device removal

When the last device in devices.conf was removed via the /remove API, the
daemon kept restarting the BT transport every reconnect_delay seconds only
to log "No devices configured". Wait on _resume_event instead so the
daemon stays idle until a new pair (which calls daemon.resume()).

Also fix remove_pairing_key, which iterated the top-level keys of
pairing_keys.json. Bumble's JsonKeyStore nests entries under a namespace
("__DEFAULT__"), so the address match never fired and link keys for
removed devices stayed in the keystore.

fix(brcm): survive UART byte loss on deep-idle wake (#120)

On the Oasis 2 a page turn after 10-30s of reading is dropped, then
recovers on its own minutes later. Two things combine to cause it.

The SoC enters cpuidle LOW-POWER-IDLE (ARM platform off, 24MHz OSC, DDR
in self-refresh), whose ~500us exit latency is far longer than the UART
RX FIFO covers at 2 Mbaud: 32 bytes is 160us of slack. The leading bytes
of the HCI packet are gone before the UART is clocked again. We make this
worse ourselves by writing proto=0 to keep the chip awake, which tears
down the HOST_WAKE IRQ, so nothing pulls the SoC out of idle ahead of the
chip's data.

Then bumble's parser turns those lost bytes into a dead session rather
than a dropped packet: it trusts the length field, so a corrupt header
claiming 8256 bytes silently swallows the next 8 KB of good HCI, and an
unknown packet type raises out of feed_data, discarding the rest of the
read.

Hold a PM QoS CPU_DMA_LATENCY ceiling while the transport is open. The
budget comes from FIFO drain time at the real baud rate, not a hardcoded
state index, so it allows WAIT (50us) and blocks LOW-POWER-IDLE (500us)
on i.MX7D and takes no hold at all where every state already fits. The fd
releases on crash and survives suspend with no bookkeeping; falls back to
the cpuidle sysfs disable flag, with restore, where the misc device is
missing.

Replace the RX parser with one that bounds every length field and resyncs
a byte at a time. It accepts only ACL and Event: this is a HID host, it
never sets up SCO or ISO, and excluding them denies noise two ways to
look like a valid header.

Also set IGNBRK on the UART. pyserial clears it on every open, so a line
break arrives as a literal 0x00 in the HCI stream and desyncs the parser.

Keyed off the chip rather than the transport spec, since an overridden or
probed config hands the same UART back as a file: spec. MediaTek Kindles
are untouched.

fix(waf): sanitize daemon log output before it reaches the debug screen

The log and pairing views render daemon log lines straight into the page.
`escapeHtml` neutralises `& < > "`, but log text also carries ANSI colour escapes
and can carry C0/C1 control bytes, and neither is touched. Those corrupt the
WebKit view this runs in.

Strip CSI sequences using the parameter, intermediate and final byte ranges from
the spec, so colon-separated SGR (`ESC[38:2:R:G:Bm`) and private parameters
(`ESC[>0c`) are covered rather than just the common `ESC[31m` form. Strip C0, DEL
and C1, keeping tab, newline and carriage return so the log stays readable.

Assign log text through a text node rather than as markup. Escaping is sufficient
for correctness; a text node is belt-and-braces, on the grounds that it cannot be
reinterpreted as markup at all, which is worth having for content the page does not
author. The message bar was also taking `innerHTML` from an unescaped argument.

`escapeHtml` now sanitizes first, so the remaining `innerHTML` call sites that go
through it benefit without changing.

The viewer is also capped at its last 6000 characters. To be clear about why: each
poll replaces the content rather than appending, and `/logs` is already bounded
server-side, so this is not fixing unbounded growth — it is a ceiling on how much
text the view has to lay out on a slow e-ink device, and the oldest lines are the
least interesting.

Verified against the built file: plain, colon-separated and private-parameter CSI
sequences are all removed; C0, DEL and the whole C1 block go; tab, newline, CR,
U+007E, NBSP and accented characters survive; null, undefined and numbers are
handled; the cap trims to 6000 keeping the tail; a realistic multi-line log sample
comes through unchanged apart from its escapes; and no log element is assigned
innerHTML any more.

fix(install,waf): update an existing install without uninstalling first

Refs #146.

Re-running the installer over a live install did not work, so the documented
workaround was to uninstall, copy the files again and reinstall. The reason is
that the running daemon holds dist/ld-linux-armhf.so.3 open for execution, so
every write to it comes back ETXTBSY. Busybox tar stops at the first entry it
cannot replace rather than skipping it, and that file is entry 8 of 120 in the
release tarball, so unpacking over a live install lands six .so files and
abandons everything else. The KindleForge package script runs under set -e and
exits right there, before the upstart job, the udev rule, the scriptlet and the
plugin are installed, while still reporting success.

Stop the daemon and wait for the loader to actually exit before touching any
files, then start it again at the end, including on the failure paths.

Files that disappear between releases were never removed, since both install
paths merged over the top. setlayout.sh, menu_setlayout.json and
event_map_keyboard.lua have all been dropped at some point and would still be
sitting there, and KOReader will happily load a stale lua file. Replace dist,
scripts, assets and koreader-plugin wholesale when installing from a staging
directory, and carry an explicit removal list for the case where the release
was unpacked straight over the install directory.

config.ini was overwritten on every install, silently discarding a customised
hci_transport or protocol. Keep the existing one and write the new defaults to
config.ini.new instead. devices.conf and cache/ were already left alone.

Detect "already at the destination" with a sentinel probe rather than by
comparing SRC_DIR to INSTALL_DIR as strings, the same way kindle-button-mapper
does. /mnt/us is case-insensitive and also reachable through the /mnt/base-us
alias mount, and here a false negative is destructive rather than merely a
same-file cp abort: the install directory gets wiped and then the copy fails,
because the source was what had just been deleted.

install-waf-app.sh and BTManager.sh both skipped registration entirely when the
handlerId already existed, so an update that moves the app or changes its
command line never took effect. The statements are already INSERT OR IGNORE and
INSERT OR REPLACE, so drop the guard and rewrite it every time. Clear the
mesquite cache too, otherwise the app keeps serving the previous version's html
and js, which is what just deploy has been doing all along.

Reload the upstart configuration after dropping the job file, a freshly written
.conf stays unknown until a reboot otherwise, so the start that follows fails.

uninstallAll now only prompts when stdin is a tty, since package managers run it
without one and have already confirmed in their own UI, and it removes the

sleeping a fixed settle time and hoping.

and a job upstart doesn't know is treated as nothing to wait for, so

  keyboard + multitouch       77 -> 31   multitouch gone, keyboard works
  multitouch only             66 -> 66   no node, same as before

needs, instead of throwing it away.

fix(install): always remount root read-only on exit

installUdevRules, installUpstart, removeUpstart and uninstallAll each open
a `mntroot rw` window. The pairs match on the happy path, but a signal
lands the script somewhere in between and leaves / mounted read-write,
and installAll also shells out to the bundled button-mapper installer,
which can abort inside its own window.

core_pattern on these devices is a bare "core", so a crashing framework
process dumps into its cwd, which for the daemons is /. Root is a 493MB
partition that already sits near full, so a few mesquite or pillowd cores
fill it and the framework stops coming up. USB mass storage only ever
exports the user store, so that state cannot be repaired from the host.

entry points, which are thin wrappers around installAll and uninstallAll.

feat(ble): report page-turner battery level over the status API

Plenty of BLE page turners expose their charge only through the standard
Battery Service, and nothing in the Kindle UI ever shows it, so once a
device is paired here there is no way to tell how much is left.

feat(plugin): show peripheral battery in the KOReader status bars

is needed. ReaderFooter:addAdditionalFooterContent registers a function
for the bottom status bar, and ReaderCoptListener:addAdditionalHeaderContent
does the same for the crengine header at the top of EPUBs. ReadTimer uses
both the same way.

refresh, so the level is cached and a scheduled poll refreshes it from

input node and stops when the last one goes away, which keeps anyone who

see a value. When several devices report, the lowest wins.

so it renders with the icon font KOReader ships rather than an emoji the
device may not have. It follows the same icons, compact and letters styles

fix(brcm): hand btd back when we power the chip off

The warm handoff SIGSTOPs btd so it cannot respawn bsa_server behind us,
and until now the only thing that ever unfroze it was _recover_btd, which
runs on a retry after a 12s warm-up timeout, not on any normal path.

So every power_off left btd stopped. A frozen btd can neither respawn
bsa_server nor answer BTenable, which is exactly what the next warm-up
needs, and `initctl restart btd` hangs on it too, so the restart at the

when btenable already read 0 we returned early and never even tried, so
btd stayed frozen with nothing left to thaw it.

blank. Pull the SIGCONT out of _recover_btd into _thaw_btd and do it
first thing in power_off, on both exits. Reported on #225, where the
controller does not come back after sleep and only a reboot clears it.

fix(classic): give an incoming peer a quiet window before we touch the link

On a reconnect the peer pages us and immediately runs its own LMP security
procedure. Everything we initiate in that window collides with it. f9fc8b1
gated the security block on role and cb0f404 gated it on the collision error
code, but both still fire the role switch request into the peer's procedure,
and testing cb0f404 on a PW6 showed that is where the damage is. Of seven
sessions, three died between 285 ms and 375 ms having only ever asked for the
role switch, and one that collided on encrypt() came up, delivered keys and
was torn down by the peer 29.9 s later on the 30 s LMP Response Timeout. The
only session that held collided on the switch and so never called encrypt()
at all. A collided procedure does not reliably continue on the peer's side.

So initiate nothing until we know whether the peer is driving. On an incoming
connection, wait up to 1 s for the peer to encrypt the link or open the HID
channels. Either signal means it is running its own procedure, so stay
peripheral, skip the switch and the security block, and give it the existing
5 s to open the channels before paging outward. An empty window means no peer
procedure to collide with, so run the old path unchanged: switch to central,
authenticate, encrypt, page the channels.

This drops peer_driving and the collision error keying entirely and folds the
separate channel wait into the same gate. A device that runs no procedure of
its own never signals, so the 8BitDo from #85 keeps the central path at the
cost of the 1 s window, well inside the 6 s it waits before giving up. The
non-collision ROLE_SWITCH_FAILED [0x35] case now drives security itself
instead of standing down for a procedure that was never running.

Also skip a redundant authenticate() when the link is already authenticated,
which was a silent 5 s stall, and warn at finalize when the link is not
encrypted, since that is what a link on its way to the 30 s timeout looks
like.

fix(uhid): keep the input node alive across a reconnect

A report written to a fresh UHID node goes nowhere. evdev only buffers
for readers that are already attached, and on a Basic 4 X opens a new
node about half a second after it appears while KOReader takes two. A
page turner that wakes on a button press sends exactly one report for
that press, so rebuilding the node on every connect eats it and the
user has to press twice.

The node now belongs to the host, keyed by address, and a session only
borrows it. Nothing is held or replayed, the readers simply never
detach. It is rebuilt when the descriptor or the configured name
changes, pruned once the device leaves config, and destroyed with the
host.

else, including fragments, other CIDs and packets while bumble is
reassembling, still takes the normal path. Routes are added when the
interrupt channel opens and dropped when it closes.

wheels and dials keep every report, since a repeat there is movement.
